title: “Secondary Axis Stability in Golf Clubs: From Bizarre Physics to Better Putters” format: html: toc: true toc-depth: 3 number-sections: false 1. Why “secondary axis stability” matters
We like to pretend the club moves around a nice clean axis:
driver: around your tilted spine
putter: around a mostly vertical axis through your shoulders
Reality is messier. The club changes shape during the swing (shaft bends, droops, lags), the hands don’t rotate perfectly about one fixed axis, and the clubhead’s mass isn’t arranged in a way that’s friendly to stable rotation.
That’s where secondary axis stability comes in:
How stable is the club’s rotation when the actual axis of motion is not one of its “nice” principal axes?
To get there, we’re going to lean on a classic rigid body phenomenon: the intermediate axis theorem (aka tennis racket theorem).

The video: “Bizarre Behavior of Rotating Bodies”

Let’s anchor the discussion on this video:
[ 
]{.quarto-shortcode__ data-is-shortcode=“1” data-raw=“{{< video https://www.youtube.com/embed/1VPfZ_XzisU

}}“}

This is the well-known “bizarre behavior of rotating bodies” demonstration: flip a rigid object in the air and it behaves fine about two axes… and goes completely weird about the third.
What’s happening is:
Any rigid body has three principal moments of inertia
I1≤I2≤I3 I 1 ​
≤I 2 ​
≤I 3 ​
, with associated orthogonal axes.
Rotation about the axes with smallest ( I1 I 1 ​
) or largest ( I3 I 3 ​
) moment is stable.
Rotation about the intermediate axis ( I2 I 2 ​
) is unstable: tiny perturbations grow into big flips.
In free flight, that instability shows up as the famous end-over-end flip. In a golf club:
The club isn’t in free flight (the hands are applying torque),
but the same structure of the equations shows up as sensitive, hard-to-control rotations when the stroke tries to use a “bad” effective axis.
That sensitivity is exactly what you feel as:
inconsistent face closure,
the head “wobbling” off-plane,
or the putter feeling fine on some strokes and alien on others.

The golf club as a changing rigid body 3.1 Principal axes of a club

For a putter head, you can roughly define:
x x-axis: pointing from face toward the back of the head
y y-axis: heel–toe direction
z z-axis: vertical
Ignoring the shaft for a moment, the head has three principal moments:
Ix I x ​
— about the face-back axis
Iy I y ​
— about the heel–toe axis
Iz I z ​
— about the vertical axis (this is the usual forgiveness MOI: resistance to twisting on off-center hits). one-putts.com +2 MDPI +2
Modern mallets push weight out to heel and toe and rearward to maximize Iz I z ​
. Typical numbers:
“Normal” putters: ~3500–6000 g·cm²
High-MOI mallets: ~6000–9000 g·cm² one-putts.com +1
That’s great for impact forgiveness, but says exactly nothing about how stable the head is when the swing axis itself is bouncing around.
3.2 Why the axis isn’t stable
In a real swing, the effective rotation axis of the clubhead is:
set by your body motion (spine tilt, secondary axis tilt, etc.), GolfWRX +2 Rotaryswing.com +2
altered by shaft bend and droop,
shifted by the fact the shaft attaches near the heel, not through the CG, Cal Poly Content +1
and influenced by how your hands “steer” the club (especially in putting).
So the axis the club actually rotates about is some ugly combination of:
your body’s rotation axis,
the shaft axis,
and whatever torque pattern your hands are applying.
That axis usually doesn’t line up with any principal axis of the head. And as the club flexes and deforms, the inertia tensor changes slightly; the principal axes move in relation to the shaft.
This is the recipe for secondary axis drama:
When the effective rotation axis drifts through the neighborhood of the intermediate principal axis, the dynamics get very sensitive.
The torque required at the hands to keep the club “behaving” can spike or change sign faster than your brain can compensate.
You won’t see a full tennis-racket flip because your hands are clamped on the thing, but you will see:
erratic closure rates,
“mysterious” pulls and pushes with what felt like the same stroke,
and a putter that feels livelier or deader depending on tiny differences in path or lie.

Secondary axis stability: a working definition

For our purposes, define secondary axis stability as:
The degree to which the club’s rotation is predictable and self-consistent when the actual swing axis is not one of the primary principal axes.
More formally:
Let I1≤I2≤I3 I 1 ​
≤I 2 ​
≤I 3 ​
be principal moments.
Let ω ω be the angular velocity of the clubhead.
If ω ω is aligned with the axis of I1 I 1 ​
or I3 I 3 ​
, rotation is naturally stable.
If ω ω lies near the intermediate axis ( I2 I 2 ​
), small perturbations in torque produce disproportionately large changes in ω ω and in the orientation of the head.
We don’t need full-blown rigid-body math here; the takeaway is:
The more your rotation axis is forced to lie in a region where the inertia tensor is “unfriendly”,
the more you’ll need fine, time-varying hand torques to keep the face stable.
A club with good secondary axis stability does two things:
It makes it hard for your effective rotation axis to wander into the “bad” intermediate regime.
When you do wander, it doesn’t punish you with violent sensitivity.

How putters are currently designed (and what they’re missing) 5.1 High-MOI, perimeter weighting

Modern mallets mostly chase maximum Iz I z ​
(vertical MOI) for impact forgiveness:
Rear and toe/heel weights,
Hollow bodies with mass pushed to the edges,
Some even approach driver-like constraints in spirit (though putters don’t share the USGA driver limit of 5900 g·cm²). Cal Poly Content +1
For off-center hits, this works: a high Iz I z ​
reduces face twist and speed loss. Argolf USA +1
But from a secondary axis perspective:
Perimeter weighting tends to make the inertia ellipsoid very “flat” in certain directions,
which can make the intermediate-axis region sharply defined and more sensitive if the swing axis passes through it.
5.2 Zero-torque and lie-angle-balanced putters
Some modern “zero-torque” or lie-angle-balanced putters attack a related issue:
They aim to align the center of mass with the shaft axis, so the torque about the shaft during the stroke is minimized. tutelman.com +2 MDPI +2
These designs greatly reduce the torque the golfer must apply to keep the face square during the stroke. That’s good.
But they still typically use some form of perimeter weighting, and they don’t explicitly target the stability of rotation when:
lie angle changes a bit,
the stroke goes slightly off-plane, or
the head flexes and the principal axes shift.
In other words: they reduce one source of “fight” (shaft torque) but don’t fully address how the head behaves when the effective rotation axis itself is wandering through secondary-axis territory.

Concept: a “secondary-axis-stable” mallet

Let’s build the concept you proposed:
A mallet putter with mass oriented on its central axis, heaviest in-plane, with light sections on the outer axis.
6.1 Geometry idea
Take a standard mallet envelope:
Heel–toe span w≈100 mm w≈100 mm
Face–back depth d≈40 mm d≈40 mm
Thickness t≈20 mm t≈20 mm
Now compare two designs with the same total mass and outer dimensions:
Perimeter design (typical high-MOI mallet)
Most mass concentrated in heel and toe wings.
Central section relatively hollow/light.
Central-axis design (your concept)
A dense “spine” along the central axis (aligned with the intended stroke plane).
Outer heel and toe regions made significantly lighter.
Optionally align the spine with the shaft insertion and swing plane, not just geometric center.
Intuitively:
Design 1 maximizes Iz I z ​
(about vertical) for forgiveness.
Design 2 reduces Iz I z ​
but brings the principal axes into closer alignment with the shaft/swing plane and makes them less sensitive to shaft flex and small lie-angle changes.

Quantifying the tradeoff: stability vs MOI

Let’s be honest: a precise calculation needs a full 3D CAD model, real material densities, and a dynamic model of the shaft + hands. I don’t have that luxury here, so I’ll show a toy but honest estimate to give you the right scale.
7.1 A simple numerical experiment
Model both heads as a grid of point masses within the same rectangular envelope:
Same overall mass and dimensions,
Only the distribution of density differs.
Assumptions:
Perimeter mallet: Outer ~60% of the heel–toe span is twice as dense as the inner region.
Central-axis mallet: A central bar (say ±15% of heel–toe span) is twice as dense, and the outer wings are made very light (e.g., 1/2 density of the center).
If you compute the inertia tensor about the center of mass and extract the principal moments (I1≤I2≤I3) (I 1 ​
≤I 2 ​
≤I 3 ​
), you get something qualitatively like:
Perimeter design (normalized units):
I1≈0.00023 I 1 ​
≈0.00023
I2≈0.00123 I 2 ​
≈0.00123
I3≈0.00133 I 3 ​
≈0.00133
Central-axis design (same mass & envelope):
I1≈0.00023 I 1 ​
≈0.00023
I2≈0.00062 I 2 ​
≈0.00062
I3≈0.00072 I 3 ​
≈0.00072
Interpretation:
The smallest moment I1 I 1 ​
(about the “long” axis) is essentially unchanged — both designs have the same basic footprint.
The largest moment I3 I 3 ​
(which you can loosely associate with vertical-axis MOI in this toy model) drops from ~0.00133 to ~0.00072.
That’s roughly:
I3,centralI3,perimeter≈0.000720.00133≈0.54 I 3,perimeter ​
I 3,central ​
​
≈ 0.00133 0.00072 ​
≈0.54
In other words:
A strong shift from perimeter weighting to central-axis weighting can cut vertical-axis MOI by about 45–50% for the same mass and size.
You can dial this up or down with less extreme weighting, but the direction of the tradeoff is clear:
More central-axis stability → less Iz I z ​
forgiveness.
7.2 Where the stability gain comes from
So why would you ever sacrifice that much MOI? Because you’re trading:
Static forgiveness at impact vs
Dynamic stability of the stroke about off-nominal axes.
Three key effects:
Axis alignment
With mass along a central spine that’s co-linear with the shaft axis and swing plane, the principal axes are more likely to stay aligned with that plane even as the shaft bends.
That means your effective rotation axis is more often close to a stable principal axis (either the min or max I I), and less likely to pass through the intermediate-axis “doom zone”.
Reduced torque variability
The torque your hands must supply to keep the face square is τ=Ieff⋅ω˙+(gyroscopic terms) τ=I eff ​
⋅ ω ˙ +(gyroscopic terms).
If the inertia tensor is more “friendly” relative to the actual stroke axis, then small path deviations or lie-angle changes cause smaller swings in effective inertia and required torque.
Practically: the putter feels like it wants to stay on its path and keep its face angle, instead of needing micro-adjustments.
Smoother behavior under shaft deflection
A perimeter mallet can have principal axes that move a lot when the shaft is bent or the lie angle changes by a few degrees.
A central-axis design tends to make the inertia tensor more axisymmetric with respect to the shaft/swing plane, so those changes have less impact on the rotational dynamics.
You’re effectively saying: “I’m willing to give up some help on bad strikes to get a stroke that’s inherently easier to keep on-plane and square.”
7.3 A rough “stability vs MOI” summary
Using the toy model as a guide (not gospel), you can imagine a family of designs:
Design type Qualitative vertical-axis MOI Qualitative secondary-axis stability Extreme perimeter mallet 100% (baseline) Poor–moderate (sensitive) Modern high-MOI zero-torque mallet 80–100% Moderate (better torque balance) Hybrid perimeter/central spine 60–80% Good Strong central-axis bias (your idea) 50–70% Very good
Those ranges are indicative, not measured. The main point is:
You probably don’t want to go all the way to a 50% MOI design for most golfers;
but a moderate central-axis bias could move you into a sweet spot where:
you lose maybe 20–30% of vertical MOI vs a full perimeter sledgehammer,
and gain a noticeable bump in how “self-stable” the stroke feels about the real, messy swing axis.

Full swing: changing shape, changing axes

Everything above is for a putter, where things are relatively tame. In a full swing, the club is:
bending, drooping, and unbending,
experiencing rapidly changing angular velocity about multiple axes,
and the shaft axis and clubhead principal axes can get badly misaligned at high speed.
In that regime, the intermediate-axis behavior from the video is lurking under the surface:
As the club’s effective inertia tensor changes during the downswing,
the “preferred” stable axes move,
and your actual angular velocity vector can drift closer to, or away from, the intermediate-axis region.
Your hands do an enormous amount of work unconsciously to keep the club behaving. That’s one reason why elite swings look effortless but are absolutely not simple mechanically.
A club designed with secondary axis stability in mind would try to:
Keep the club’s principal axes as “friendly” as possible to the actual path and shaft deflections used in the swing,
so that the club wants to move in the way your body is trying to move it, instead of constantly demanding corrections.
That’s a much harder design problem than “make Iz I z ​
big,” but the physics is the same.

Practical implications for a secondary-axis-stable mallet

If you actually built the putter we just described, here’s what you’d expect:
Pros
Stroke feels more “rail-like”: once you set it in motion, it wants to keep rotating in the same plane.
Less sensitivity to small changes in lie angle or shaft lean during the stroke.
Reduced “wobble” when the hands get a bit out of sync; the putter head behaves more like a single solid axis system.
Potentially simpler, more repeatable face-angle control for players who struggle with face rotation.
Cons
Less built-in forgiveness on mishits — especially for heel–toe strikes.
Marketing nightmare: MOI numbers would look worse on the spec sheet, even if the dynamic stability is better.
Tuning is player-specific: the “right” amount of central weighting depends on stroke style (straight-back-straight-through vs strong arc), lie angle, and shaft insertion geometry.
Who might benefit most?
Players who already strike the ball consistently near the sweet spot,
but fight face control and path consistency under pressure.
Better players who can tolerate a small drop in static forgiveness in exchange for a stroke that feels mechanically “locked in”.

Where this idea fits in the current landscape

The industry has already moved:
From “feel” blades → high-MOI mallets for forgiveness,
Into “zero-torque” and lie-angle-balanced designs that reduce shaft torque and face twist. tutelman.com +2 MDPI +2
The next logical step is exactly what you’re describing:
Putters designed not just for MOI and torque balance, but for stability with respect to the real, messy, changing swing axis — i.e., true secondary axis stability.
That means optimizing:
the full 3D inertia tensor of the head + shaft,
across a range of realistic shaft deflections and lie angles,
to keep the effective stroke axis in a dynamically stable region and to minimize torque variability at the hands.
It’s a more subtle, physics-heavy design space… which is probably why you don’t see it on marketing posters yet.

Summary (for your readers)

The YouTube video on bizarre rotating bodies shows that rotation is only naturally stable about the smallest and largest principal axes. The middle one is an unstable troublemaker.
Golf clubs, especially in motion, don’t rotate about a neat, fixed axis. Shaft flex, body motion, and off-center attachment mean the actual rotation axis wanders, sometimes into that unstable intermediate territory.
Most current putter design focuses on maximizing vertical MOI for impact forgiveness and, more recently, reducing shaft torque (zero-torque, lie-angle balanced). Those are good things but don’t fully address secondary axis stability.
A mallet with mass concentrated along a central spine aligned with the swing plane and shaft can reduce sensitivity to small changes in lie angle and shaft deflection — improving secondary axis stability.
A strong shift from perimeter to central-axis weighting can easily cut vertical-axis MOI by ~40–50% for the same mass and footprint in simple models. That’s a real tradeoff: you’re swapping some impact forgiveness for a stroke that behaves more predictably in 3D.
The smart play is probably not an extreme design, but a hybrid: enough perimeter mass to maintain respectable MOI, plus a robust central spine to tame the secondary axis chaos.
In short: we’ve spent decades making putters that forgive bad impact; the next frontier is making putters that forgive the messy way humans actually move.

This document outlines practical applications of the control-affine decomposition used in modern multibody golf swing analysis. The decomposition
\[
F_{\text{total}} = F_{\mathrm{drift}} + F_{\mathrm{input}}
\]

The material here complements Sections 1–7 by linking theory to practical biomechanics contexts, including the insights developed in prior work on momentum-driven interaction forces.

title: Applications of the Control-Affine Framework in Golf Swing Biomechanics
text:
Counterfactual Analysis (ZTCF)
The Zero Torque Counterfactual (ZTCF) isolates passive mechanical effects by evolving the system under
\[
u(t) \equiv 0.
\]
The resulting drift wrench reflects inertial, gravitational, Coriolis, centrifugal, and elastic shaft forces. This is essential for interpreting measured hand–club interaction forces and determining how much of the measured signal arises from momentum transfer rather than active muscular effort.

title: Applications of the Control-Affine Framework in Golf Swing Biomechanics
text:
Estimating Active Effort
Given measured or simulated total force \(F_{\text{total}}\), and drift force \(F_{\mathrm{drift}}\) from ZTCF-based computation, input forces are obtained via
\[
F_{\mathrm{input}} = F_{\text{total}} - F_{\mathrm{drift}}.
\]
This supports reconstruction of active joint torques, improved inverse dynamics, and isolation of the golfer’s actual contribution to club acceleration.

title: Applications of the Control-Affine Framework in Golf Swing Biomechanics
text:
Shaft Mechanics
Shaft deformation contributes only to drift and not to the input mapping. Shaft-related forces should therefore not be interpreted as direct indicators of muscular effort. Changes in stiffness or material properties primarily influence the drift term.

title: Applications of the Control-Affine Framework in Golf Swing Biomechanics
text:
Simulation and Validation
The affine formulation supports: - torque estimation through forward-dynamics matching,

counterfactual mechanical tests,
player-specific simulations based on geometry and inertial parameters.

title: Applications of the Control-Affine Framework in Golf Swing Biomechanics
text:
Data Interpretation
The decomposition provides a rigorous basis for interpreting measured forces, enabling one to classify contributions into passive, active, and constraint-filtered components. This mitigates common misinterpretations where passive effects are inaccurately attributed to active torques.

title: Applications of the Control-Affine Framework in Golf Swing Biomechanics
text:
Machine Learning Applications
ML models can be trained on drift-free input data, improving sample efficiency and interpretability. Drift can also be modeled directly to accelerate simulation, while input torques can be learned as low-dimensional latent representations.

Summary
The control-affine decomposition provides actionable guidance for simulation, measurement interpretation, torque reconstruction, shaft mechanics, and ML-based modeling. The separation of drift and input forces yields a rigorous framework for analyzing and understanding the golf swing.

title: Affine Control Interpretation of the Golf Swing: Drift, Input, and Causal Decomposition of Forces - Part I: Theoretical Foundations
text: The golf swing is a high-speed, full-body motion executed by a mechanically complex, constrained multibody system. Conventional inverse dynamics can estimate generalized joint torques and hand forces from motion capture and external force measurements, but it cannot distinguish how much of those forces arise from the golfer’s active muscular effort versus passive mechanical dynamics such as inertia, gravity, and shaft deformation. This paper develops a strictly theoretical framework that models the golfer–club–shaft system as a nonlinear control-affine mechanical system and uses that structure to decompose forces into drift (passive) and input (torque-driven) components. We define the Zero Torque Counterfactual (ZTCF) and Zero Velocity Counterfactual (ZVCF) as mathematical tools for isolating passive dynamics and torque effectiveness, and we derive a force taxonomy that classifies measured forces by their causal origin within the model. Applications and empirical validation will be presented in subsequent simulation and experimental papers.

title: Affine Control Interpretation of the Golf Swing: Drift, Input, and Causal Decomposition of Forces - Part I: Theoretical Foundations
text:
Introduction
{#sec-intro}
The golf swing is a high-speed, full-body motion executed by a mechanically complex, constrained multibody system. Traditional biomechanical analyses rely heavily on inverse dynamics to estimate generalized joint torques and hand forces from measured kinematics and external forces. While inverse dynamics provides the total generalized forces consistent with a given motion, it does not reveal the causal structure of those forces—specifically, how much arises from the golfer’s active muscular effort versus how much is generated passively by inertia, gravity, elastic shaft deformation, and motion history.
This distinction is fundamental. Passive forces (drift) can be large—even dominant—during rapid phases of the swing, meaning that inverse-dynamics forces are often misinterpreted as indicators of muscular effort. Without a principled decomposition, it is impossible to determine whether a large observed torque is caused by the golfer’s action or simply emerges from the dynamics of the system.
The aim of this manuscript is to establish a rigorous, strictly theoretical foundation for decomposing forces in the golf swing into two analytically distinct components: - Drift forces arising purely from passive, state-dependent mechanical dynamics, and

Input forces arising solely from actively applied joint torques.

The key mathematical observation is that the golfer–club–shaft system can be modeled as a nonlinear control-affine mechanical system. Control-affine systems admit an additive decomposition of their dynamics into passive drift and linear control input channels. Once the affine structure is established, counterfactual tools such as the Zero Torque Counterfactual (ZTCF) and Zero Velocity Counterfactual (ZVCF) follow naturally and enable clean mechanical attribution of forces within the model.
This paper is Part I of a broader project. It develops the theoretical architecture only—no simulation, numerical results, or empirical data are presented here. Subsequent papers (Parts II and III) will implement and validate this framework using high-fidelity multibody simulations, flexible-shaft modeling, and experimental motion-capture data. By isolating the theory in this manuscript, we ensure that the mathematical structure is complete, self-contained, and available for independent scrutiny before numerical or empirical layers are added.
The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section~[@sec:system] defines the golfer–club–shaft system, the modeling assumptions, and the state and input variables. Section~[@sec:affine] derives the unified control-affine form for the coupled rigid–flexible system. Section~[@sec:drift_input] formalizes the drift–input decomposition. Sections~[@sec:ztcf] and~[@sec:zvcf] introduce the ZTCF and ZVCF constructions. Section~[@sec:drift_invariance] discusses drift invariance and input constraints. Section~[@sec:taxonomy] presents a force taxonomy based on the affine mapping. Section~[@sec:limitations] summarizes the theoretical limitations of the framework, and Section~[@sec:conclusion] concludes with directions for future theoretical and empirical work. Detailed derivations, modal approximations, and toy examples are collected in the Appendices.

title: Affine Control Interpretation of the Golf Swing: Drift, Input, and Causal Decomposition of Forces - Part I: Theoretical Foundations
text:
System Definition and Modeling Assumptions
{#sec-system}
In this section we define the mathematical structure of the golfer–club–shaft system and state the modeling assumptions that bound the theoretical framework. The goal is not to fix a unique anatomical model but to specify a general class of multibody systems for which the subsequent analysis is valid.

Modeling assumptions
{#subsec:assumptions}

Modeling Assumptions for the Theoretical Framework\ These assumptions apply strictly to the theoretical decomposition presented in this manuscript (Part~I). They define the mathematical boundaries of the model; empirical validation and relaxation of these assumptions will be addressed in later work. 1. Rigid body segments. All anatomical segments of the golfer (torso, arms, hands) are modeled as rigid bodies with fixed mass and inertia properties.


Flexible shaft via finite-dimensional modal approximation. The shaft is modeled using ( m ) vibration modes obtained from standard beam theory (e.g., Euler–Bernoulli or Timoshenko). Modal truncation approximates the distributed dynamics with a finite-dimensional representation.
No ball–club impact phase. Ball impact is excluded from the domain of analysis due to its hybrid (non-smooth) dynamics. The model applies to the pre-impact and post-impact phases only.
No aerodynamic forces. Drag and lift forces on the clubhead and shaft are omitted in this theoretical treatment. All modeled external forces arise from gravity or internal mechanical interactions.
Torques treated as generalized inputs. Muscular physiology (activation dynamics, force–velocity, force–length, tendon elasticity) is abstracted into a net generalized torque vector ( = B u ). These torques serve as the control inputs in the affine control formulation. The set of admissible torques may be state-dependent in practice; here we treat (u) as an exogenous input signal at the mechanical level.
Ground contact modeled as holonomic constraint. Feet–ground interaction is simplified as a fixed base with no slip or compliance; the golfer is treated as rooted at the ground.
Smooth dynamical evolution (no discontinuities). Between impacts, the system evolves via smooth ordinary differential equations. Shaft deformation and all segmental interactions are continuous in time.
No measurement noise or parameter uncertainty. The theoretical decomposition assumes perfect state knowledge and exact model parameters. Sensitivity to uncertainty and noise is a topic for subsequent empirical work.



Generalized coordinates and state
{#subsec:coords_state}
The golfer’s anatomy is modeled as a multibody kinematic chain with
\[
  q \in \R^{n}
\]
generalized coordinates, each representing a rotational degree of freedom (e.g., shoulder rotations, elbow flexion, wrist deviations, spinal rotations). Any standard representation (Denavit–Hartenberg parameters, exponential coordinates, or spatial vectors) is admissible.
The flexible shaft is modeled via a finite-dimensional modal approximation with modal coordinates
\[
  \eta = [\eta_{1}, \dots, \eta_{m}]^{T} \in \R^{m},
\]
where each ( _{i} ) represents the amplitude of a particular bending or deformation mode.
We define the full state vector as
\[
  x = [q^{T}, \qd^{T}, \eta^{T}, \etad^{T}]^{T} \in \R^{2(n+m)}.
\]
This state structure is chosen to support the drift vector field ( f(x) ) and input vector fields ( g(x) ) introduced later.


Torque inputs and actuation mapping
{#subsec:inputs}
Muscular torques are abstracted as control inputs
\[
  u \in \R^{m_{u}}, \quad m_{u} \leq n,
\]
with
\[
  \tau = B(q)\, u,
\]
where ( ^{n} ) is the generalized joint torque vector and ( B(q) ^{n m_{u}} ) encodes actuation pathways and moment arms. In the simplest case, (B) is constant; more generally, it may depend on configuration. In either case, torques enter linearly in the equations of motion.
Throughout this paper we treat (u) as the exogenous input at the mechanical level. The mapping from neural commands to (u) is outside the scope of this theoretical work.


External forces and constraints
{#subsec:external_forces}
External forces included in the model are: - gravitational loading,

inertial, Coriolis, and centrifugal effects arising from the multibody kinematics,
passive joint contributions (if modeled explicitly),
elastic and damping forces from shaft deformation. Aerodynamic forces, impact forces, and non-holonomic contact effects are excluded under the assumptions of Section~[@subsec:assumptions]. Ground contact is modeled as a holonomic constraint that effectively fixes the base of the kinematic chain.



Hand–club kinematic interface
{#subsec:hand_club}
Let ( r_{h}(q) ) denote the hand pose (e.g., the pose of a marker cluster or a grip reference frame) and ( r_{}(q,) ) the clubhead pose. Under a modal shaft approximation, the clubhead pose can be written schematically as
\[
  r_{\text{club}}(q,\eta) = r_{h}(q) + \sum_{i=1}^{m} \phi_{i} \, \eta_{i},
\]
where ( _{i} ) are mode-shape dependent vectors (or fields, in a more detailed representation). This coupling modifies the inertia, Coriolis, and elastic terms in the dynamics but does not introduce multiplicative torque terms; the control input still enters linearly through the joint torques.


Notation table
{#subsec:notation}
For reference, Table~[@tab:notation] summarizes the main symbols used in the manuscript.

title: Affine Control Interpretation of the Golf Swing: Drift, Input, and Causal Decomposition of Forces - Part I: Theoretical Foundations
text:
Unified Control-Affine Derivation (Rigid + Flexible System)
{#sec-affine}
We now establish the control-affine structure of the coupled golfer–club–shaft system. The derivation presented here is concise; detailed algebraic expansions, block-matrix forms, and modal–rigid coupling expressions are relegated to Appendix~[@app:derivations].

Equations of motion
Let (q ^{n}) and (^{m}) denote the rigid-body and shaft modal coordinates, respectively, and let [ v =
\[\begin{bmatrix} \qd \\ \etad \end{bmatrix}\]
] collect their velocities. The multibody equations of motion for the coupled system can be written in the standard form
\[
  M(q,\eta)
  \begin{bmatrix}
    \qdd \\[0.2em]
    \etadd
  \end{bmatrix}
  +
  C(q,\qd,\eta,\etad)
  \begin{bmatrix}
    \qd \\[0.2em]
    \etad
  \end{bmatrix}
  + G(q) +
  \begin{bmatrix}
    0 \\[0.2em]
    K_{s}\eta + C_{s}\etad
  \end{bmatrix}
  =
  \begin{bmatrix}
    \tau \\[0.2em]
    0
  \end{bmatrix},
  {#eq-eom_block}
\]
where: - (M(q,)) is the inertia matrix for the coupled rigid–flexible system,

(C(q,,,)) encodes Coriolis and centrifugal effects,
(G(q)) is the gravitational torque vector,
(K_{s}) and (C_{s}) are the shaft stiffness and damping matrices,
(= B(q) u) is the generalized torque vector induced by control inputs (u). The shaft degrees of freedom have no direct torque inputs; all shaft forces are passive (elastic and damping).

Equation~\(\eqref{eq:eom_block}\) is schematic but captures the structural separation between passive mechanical effects and torque inputs.


Solving for accelerations
Assuming (M(q,)) is nonsingular, we may solve for the accelerations:
\[
  \begin{bmatrix}
    \qdd \\[0.2em]
    \etadd
  \end{bmatrix}
  =
  - M^{-1}(q,\eta)
  \left(
    C(q,\qd,\eta,\etad)
    \begin{bmatrix}
      \qd \\[0.2em]
      \etad
    \end{bmatrix}
    + G(q) +
    \begin{bmatrix}
      0 \\[0.2em]
      K_{s}\eta + C_{s}\etad
    \end{bmatrix}
  \right)
  +
  M^{-1}(q,\eta)
  \begin{bmatrix}
    B(q)\,u \\[0.2em]
    0
  \end{bmatrix}.
  {#eq-accel_split}
\]
Everything not multiplied by (u) is passive; the term proportional to (u) is the torque-driven component.
Define the drift acceleration
\[
  a_{\text{drift}}(x)
  =
  - M^{-1}(q,\eta)
  \left(
    C(q,\qd,\eta,\etad)
    \begin{bmatrix}
      \qd \\[0.2em]
      \etad
    \end{bmatrix}
    + G(q) +
    \begin{bmatrix}
      0 \\[0.2em]
      K_{s}\eta + C_{s}\etad
    \end{bmatrix}
  \right),
\]
and the input acceleration mapping
\[
  A_{\text{input}}(x)
  =
  M^{-1}(q,\eta)
  \begin{bmatrix}
    B(q) \\[0.2em]
    0
  \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Then~\(\eqref{eq:accel_split}\) becomes
\[
  \begin{bmatrix}
    \qdd \\[0.2em]
    \etadd
  \end{bmatrix}
  =
  a_{\text{drift}}(x) + A_{\text{input}}(x)\,u.
\]


First-order state-space form
We now express the dynamics in first-order form. Recall
\[
  x = [q^{T}, \qd^{T}, \eta^{T}, \etad^{T}]^{T}.
\]
The state derivative is
\[
  \xd =
  \begin{bmatrix}
    \qd \\[0.2em]
    \qdd \\[0.2em]
    \etad \\[0.2em]
    \etadd
  \end{bmatrix}
  =
  f(x) + g(x)\,u,
  {#eq-affine_state}
\]
where
\[
  f(x) =
  \begin{bmatrix}
    \qd \\[0.2em]
    [a_{\text{drift}}(x)]_{1:n} \\[0.2em]
    \etad \\[0.2em]
    [a_{\text{drift}}(x)]_{n+1:n+m}
  \end{bmatrix},
  \qquad
  g(x) =
  \begin{bmatrix}
    0 \\[0.2em]
    [A_{\text{input}}(x)]_{1:n,:} \\[0.2em]
    0 \\[0.2em]
    [A_{\text{input}}(x)]_{n+1:n+m,:}
  \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Here ([]{1:n}) and ([]{n+1:n+m}) denote the rigid and flexible components of the acceleration, and ([]_{:, :}) denotes the appropriate block of the input matrix.
Equation~\(\eqref{eq:affine_state}\) is a nonlinear control-affine system:
\[
  \xd = f(x) + g(x)\,u.
\]
All nonlinearities—including those introduced by shaft flexibility—are contained in the drift vector field (f(x)), while the input vector fields (g(x)) multiply the control input (u) linearly. The purely rigid-body model is recovered by setting (m = 0).


Structural consequences
Three structural observations follow: 1. Flexibility enriches drift but preserves input linearity. Shaft flexibility introduces additional passive degrees of freedom and modifies (M, C,) and the elastic terms, but all shaft forces remain in the drift. The control input still enters linearly through joint torques.

All torque-driven effects are confined to (g(x)u). Any change in the dynamics caused by altering the torque profile must pass through the input term; the drift term depends only on the state and parameters.
The affine structure is independent of parameter values. The decomposition does not rely on particular numerical values of masses, inertias, or shaft stiffness, only on the linearity of torque in the equations of motion. In practice, parameter uncertainty affects the accuracy of the decomposition but not its algebraic form.

This control-affine structure is the backbone for the drift–input decomposition and the counterfactual constructions developed in the next sections.

title: Affine Control Interpretation of the Golf Swing: Drift, Input, and Causal Decomposition of Forces - Part I: Theoretical Foundations
text:
Drift vs. Input Decomposition
{#sec-drift_input}
Given the control-affine form~\(\eqref{eq:affine_state}\), we now formalize the separation of passive (drift) and active (input) contributions to the dynamics.

Passive drift dynamics
The drift dynamics are defined as the evolution of the system in the absence of all muscular torques:
\[
  \xd_{\text{drift}} = f(x).
\]
Physically, this includes: - inertia of all rigid segments,

Coriolis and centrifugal forces,
gravitational torques,
passive joint contributions (if modeled),
elastic and damping forces from shaft deformation. Drift represents what the system would do “on its own” given its current configuration, velocities, and shaft deformation, under the modeling assumptions of Section~[@subsec:assumptions].



Torque-driven input dynamics
The input dynamics are defined as the torque-driven component:
\[
  \xd_{\text{input}} = g(x)\,u.
\]
Key properties: - The dependence on (u) is strictly linear.

The mapping (g(x)) depends on configuration and shaft deformation, but does not multiply (u) nonlinearly.
The number of effective torque channels is (m_{u} n), reflecting anatomical underactuation at the joint level. This term represents the portion of the dynamics directly caused by the golfer’s applied torques at the mechanical level of description.



Total evolution and causal interpretation within the model
Combining the two contributions yields
\[
  \xd = f(x) + g(x)\,u = \xd_{\text{drift}} + \xd_{\text{input}}.
\]
Within the model, this additive structure supports the following interpretation: - the drift term (f(x)) captures the passive mechanical response to the current state,

the input term (g(x)u) captures the incremental effect of the applied torques on top of that passive response. The decomposition is analytically exact for the chosen multibody model; in practice it is limited by parameter accuracy and the validity of the modeling assumptions.



Role in counterfactual analysis
The drift–input decomposition underlies the counterfactual tools introduced later: - The Zero Torque Counterfactual (ZTCF) trajectory integrates the drift-only dynamics from a given initial state, isolating the passive evolution of the system.

The Zero Velocity Counterfactual (ZVCF) evaluates forces at the same configuration with velocities set to zero, isolating configuration-dependent contributions. By comparing total forces to these counterfactual constructions via inverse dynamics, we can separate drift and input forces and construct a force taxonomy for interpretation of measured or simulated swings.

title: Affine Control Interpretation of the Golf Swing: Drift, Input, and Causal Decomposition of Forces - Part I: Theoretical Foundations
text:
Zero Torque Counterfactual (ZTCF)
{#sec-ztcf}
The drift–input decomposition in~\(\eqref{eq:affine_state}\) separates the dynamics into a passive component (f(x)) and a torque-driven component (g(x)u). The Zero Torque Counterfactual (ZTCF) formalizes the idea of “what the system would have done under identical conditions if the golfer had applied no torques at all.” It is defined strictly within the mechanical model and is used as a reference against which the actual, torque-driven motion can be compared.

Definition as a drift-only trajectory
Consider the control-affine system
\[
  \xd = f(x) + g(x)\,u, \qquad x(t_{0}) = x_{0}.
  {#eq-affine_repeat}
\]
Let (x(t)) denote the actual trajectory of the system under some torque input (u(t)) on a time interval (t ), with the initial condition
\[
  x(t_{0}) = x_{0}.
\]
We define the Zero Torque Counterfactual trajectory, denoted (x^{}(t)), as the solution of the drift-only system
\[
  \dot{x}^{\mathrm{ZTCF}}(t) = f\big(x^{\mathrm{ZTCF}}(t)\big), \qquad x^{\mathrm{ZTCF}}(t_{0}) = x_{0},
  {#eq-ztcf_def}
\]
on the same time interval ([t_{0}, t_{f}]).
By construction: - The initial condition is identical to that of the actual swing.

All mechanical parameters (masses, inertias, shaft stiffness, etc.) are identical.
The only difference is that the torque input is set to zero: (u(t) ). Thus (x^{}(t)) is the unique trajectory predicted by the model when the system is released from the same initial state but allowed to evolve purely under passive dynamics.



Relationship to drift and input terms
Along the actual trajectory (x(t)), the state derivative is
\[
  \dot{x}(t) = f\big(x(t)\big) + g\big(x(t)\big)\,u(t),
\]
while along the ZTCF trajectory (x^{}(t)) the derivative is purely
\[
  \dot{x}^{\mathrm{ZTCF}}(t) = f\big(x^{\mathrm{ZTCF}}(t)\big).
\]
The drift vector field (f(x)) is invariant with respect to the instantaneous torque input: it depends only on the state and model parameters, not on (u). In contrast, the input term (g(x)u) vanishes identically when (u = 0).
Conceptually, ZTCF isolates the drift dynamics by providing a full trajectory that is generated only by (f(x)). The difference between the actual trajectory and its ZTCF counterpart, when interpreted via the equations of motion, captures the incremental effect of the torque input.


Using ZTCF with inverse dynamics
In practice, we are often given a measured or simulated swing trajectory in terms of kinematics,
\[
  \big(q(t), \qd(t), \eta(t), \etad(t)\big), \qquad t \in [t_{0}, t_{f}],
\]
and we obtain the generalized torque vector (_{}(t)) from inverse dynamics:
\[
  \tau_{\text{total}}(t) = \text{ID}\big(q(t), \qd(t), \qdd(t), \eta(t), \etad(t), \etadd(t)\big),
\]
where (()) denotes the inverse dynamics operator for the coupled rigid–flexible model.
From the equations of motion~\(\eqref{eq:eom_block}\), the generalized torques can be written as
\[
  \tau_{\text{total}}(t)
  =
  \underbrace{\tau_{\text{drift}}\big(x(t)\big)}_{\text{passive component}}
  +
  \underbrace{\tau_{\text{input}}(t)}_{\text{torque-driven component}},
  {#eq-tau_split}
\]
where the drift torque is defined by evaluating the passive terms at the actual state:
\[
  \tau_{\text{drift}}\big(x(t)\big)
  =
  M_{q}(q,\eta)\,\big[a_{\text{drift}}(x(t))\big]_{1:n},
\]
and (M_{q}) denotes the block of the inertia matrix mapping rigid accelerations to generalized torques (see Appendix~[@app:derivations] for details).
The input torque is then given by
\[
  \tau_{\text{input}}(t)
  =
  \tau_{\text{total}}(t) - \tau_{\text{drift}}\big(x(t)\big).
  {#eq-tau_input_def}
\]
Equations~\(\eqref{eq:tau_split}\)–\(\eqref{eq:tau_input_def}\) provide an algebraically exact decomposition of the total generalized torque into drift and input components within the model.
The ZTCF trajectory is not strictly required to compute this decomposition: evaluating the drift terms (a_{}(x)) along the actual trajectory (x(t)) is sufficient. However, the ZTCF provides a useful conceptual and computational tool: - Conceptually, it is the trajectory that realizes the drift dynamics in isolation.

Computationally, simulating (x^{}(t)) gives a concrete motion that can be analyzed or visualized alongside the actual swing to illustrate the effect of the torque input.



Interpretational scope and limitations
The ZTCF is a counterfactual within the model. It answers the question: > “Given the same initial configuration, velocities, shaft deformation, and model parameters, what motion would the system execute if all muscular torques were set to zero?”
It does not claim that such a motion could actually be achieved by a real golfer, nor that the nervous system ever selects “zero torque” as a control policy during a swing. Instead, ZTCF is a mathematical device that: - isolates the passive mechanical contribution to the dynamics,

provides a baseline against which torque-driven effects can be quantified, and
makes the drift–input decomposition explicit and reproducible.

All causal statements made in this paper are therefore conditional on the mechanical model and on the modeling assumptions in Section~[@subsec:assumptions]. Within that scope, the decomposition [ {}(t) = {}(x(t)) + _{}(t) ] and the associated ZTCF construction are analytically exact. Outside that scope, their interpretation must be made with care and with explicit reference to model fidelity, parameter uncertainty, and unmodeled physiological effects.

title: Affine Control Interpretation of the Golf Swing: Drift, Input, and Causal Decomposition of Forces - Part I: Theoretical Foundations
text:
Zero Velocity Counterfactual (ZVCF)
{#sec-zvcf}
The Zero Velocity Counterfactual (ZVCF) isolates configuration-dependent forces by evaluating the system at the same configuration as the actual swing but with all generalized velocities set to zero. Whereas the ZTCF is a trajectory-level counterfactual that simulates the drift dynamics forward in time, the ZVCF is an instantaneous construction. It identifies the passive mechanical forces that arise only from configuration (such as gravity and elastic shaft deformation), without contributions from inertial, Coriolis, or velocity-dependent damping terms.

Definition
Let the actual swing at time (t) be characterized by the state [ x(t) = (q(t),, (t),, (t),, (t)). ] The Zero Velocity Counterfactual state at the same instant is defined as
\[
  x^{\mathrm{ZVCF}}(t)
  =
  \big(q(t),\, 0,\, \eta(t),\, 0\big).
  {#eq-zvcf_state}
\]
Only the configuration variables (q(t)) and ((t)) are retained; all generalized velocities are set to zero.
Evaluating the equations of motion at this state yields the ZVCF generalized torque:
\[
  \tau_{\mathrm{ZVCF}}(t)
  =
  \text{ID}\!\left(q(t),\, 0,\,
  \eta(t),\, 0,\,
  \qdd^{\mathrm{ZVCF}}(t),\,
  \etadd^{\mathrm{ZVCF}}(t)\right)
  {#eq-zvcf_id}
\]
where the ZVCF accelerations are computed from the passive terms of the dynamics evaluated at zero velocity:
\[
  \begin{bmatrix}
    \qdd^{\mathrm{ZVCF}} \\[0.2em]
    \etadd^{\mathrm{ZVCF}}
  \end{bmatrix}
  =
  a_{\text{drift}}\big(q(t),0,\eta(t),0\big).
  {#eq-zvcf_accel}
\]
Intuitively, (_{}(t)) represents the generalized torques the model predicts at that configuration if: - the system were held momentarily at rest,

the shaft retained its instantaneous deformation ((t)),
but no velocity-dependent forces were present.



What ZVCF isolates
Evaluating the drift terms at zero velocity eliminates: - Coriolis and centrifugal forces (all terms proportional to () or ()),

velocity-proportional damping in the shaft,
any passive joint damping,
all torque input contributions.

What remains in (_{}(t)) are: - gravitational torques (G(q)),

elastic shaft restoring forces (K_s (t)),
configuration-dependent components of the multibody dynamics (e.g., coupling due to mass distribution),
geometric projection effects (due to Jacobians and inertia coupling).

Thus the ZVCF isolates forces arising purely from the system’s instantaneous shape.


Relation to ZTCF and drift–input decomposition
ZVCF and ZTCF play complementary roles: - ZTCF (trajectory-level) removes torque input but preserves velocity, allowing inertial, history-dependent drift forces to act naturally.

ZVCF (instantaneous) removes all velocity contributions, freezing the system in place to expose purely configuration-dependent loads.

Within the drift–input decomposition, [ {}(t) = {}(t) + {}(t), ] the ZVCF satisfies [ {}(t) = _{}(q(t),0,(t),0), ] so ZVCF should be viewed as the zero-velocity slice of the drift torque field.
The full drift torque can be written as
\[
  \tau_{\text{drift}}(t)
  =
  \tau_{\mathrm{ZVCF}}(t)
  +
  \tau_{\mathrm{vel.\,drift}}(t),
  {#eq-zvcf_split}
\]
where (_{}(t)) contains all velocity-dependent passive forces (Coriolis, centrifugal, shaft damping, etc.).


Interpretational cautions
The ZVCF is not intended to represent a physically realizable motion: - A real golfer cannot instantaneously set all joint and shaft velocities to zero while holding the same configuration.

The system would generally not remain in equilibrium under (_{}(t)); internal and external forces would cause instantaneous acceleration.

Instead, ZVCF is a mathematical probe of the model used to answer: > “At this exact configuration, ignoring all motion, what passive torques does the system geometry and shaft deformation impose?”
This makes it especially useful for: - quantifying shaft bending loads independent of motion history,

separating gravity from inertial effects,
identifying configuration-driven mechanical biases (e.g., favored directions of passive motion),
analyzing torque effectiveness by comparing total torque to ZVCF and ZTCF baselines.

ZVCF therefore complements ZTCF in building a full picture of drift forces across both configuration and velocity dimensions.

title: Affine Control Interpretation of the Golf Swing: Drift, Input, and Causal Decomposition of Forces - Part I: Theoretical Foundations
text:
Drift Invariance and Input Constraints
{#sec-drift_invariance}
The drift–input decomposition
\[
  \xd = f(x) + g(x)u
\]
is meaningful only if the drift term (f(x)) is invariant with respect to the instantaneous torque input. This section formalizes that property and explains its consequences. We also discuss input constraints and their impact on the decomposition.

Definition of drift invariance
The drift vector field (f(x)) is said to be input-invariant if
\[
  f(x) \ \text{is independent of} \ u,
  {#eq-drift_invariance_def}
\]
for all states (x) in the domain of interest.
For mechanical systems with generalized torques entering linearly, [ = M^{-1}(q,)(- h(q,,,)), ] where (h()) collects all passive terms, linearity of () ensures that
\[
  a_{\text{drift}}(x)
  =
  -M^{-1}(q,\eta)\,h(q,\qd,\eta,\etad)
  {#eq-drift_terms}
\]
contains no torque dependence.
Thus,
\[
  f(x) =
  \begin{bmatrix}
    \qd \\ a_{\text{drift}}(x) \\ \etad \\ [a_{\text{drift}}(x)]_{\text{flex}}
  \end{bmatrix}
\]
is an intrinsic property of the system’s geometry, inertia, shaft deformation, and velocities, but not of the applied torques.
This invariance is what makes ZTCF (Section~[@sec:ztcf]) a well-defined counterfactual: setting (u=0) removes the input term entirely, with no hidden torque dependence remaining inside (f(x)).


Consequences of drift invariance
Drift invariance has three key consequences for the force decomposition.

(1) Passive and active forces are formally separable.
The total generalized torque from inverse dynamics satisfies [ {}(t) = {}(x(t)) + {}(t), ] where ({}) is computed by evaluating the passive terms at the actual state.
Because (f(x)) is input-invariant, (_{}) depends only on the state and model parameters, not on the golfer’s actions.


(2) Torque effectiveness can be evaluated cleanly.
Comparisons between [ {}(t),{}(t),{}(t),{}(t) ] are meaningful because the drift component is unaffected by any instantaneous torque adjustment.
This allows ZVCF and ZTCF to serve as consistent baselines.


(3) Parameter changes affect drift, control changes do not.
Any modification to: - segment masses or inertias,

shaft stiffness or damping,
kinematic constraints,
anthropometry, changes (f(x)).

In contrast, changing the torque profile (u(t)) leaves (f(x)) unchanged.
This separation is the foundation for counterfactual analysis, optimization of torque profiles, and sensitivity studies.



Velocity dependence vs. torque dependence
Although the drift is independent of torque, it may depend strongly on velocity.
In particular, - Coriolis and centrifugal forces scale with velocity,

shaft damping and flexible-body coupling can depend on (),
inertial coupling between segments depends on motion history.

Thus, drift invariance means: [ f(x)   u, , . ]
This distinction motivates the role of ZVCF, which isolates the configuration-dependent subset of drift forces by removing all velocity dependence.


Input constraints
{#subsec:input_constraints}
The affine structure admits input constraints of the form
\[
  u(t) \in \mathcal{U}(x(t)),
  {#eq-input_constraints}
\]
where ((x)) may depend on configuration or state.
For example: - joint torque limits that vary with posture,

strength reductions near extreme joint angles,
actuation limits from tendon moment arms,
bilateral couplings or coordination constraints.

These constraints do not break the affine structure.
They restrict the admissible inputs but leave [ f(x) g(x) ] unchanged.
Thus, even with realistic physiological limitations, - the decomposition ( = f(x) + g(x)u ) remains valid,

the torque decomposition ( {} = {} + _{} ) remains valid,
ZTCF and ZVCF remain fully defined,
causal attributions remain meaningful within the model.



Interpretational scope
Drift invariance enables strong causal statements, but only within the mechanical model.
Real neuromuscular systems impose: - activation dynamics,

delays,
coupling between muscle groups,
physiological force limits,
state-dependent strength variations.

These appear in the present framework only through the feasible input set ((x)).
The affine decomposition is agnostic to the internal physiology; it models only the net mechanical torque transmitted to the joints.
Interpretations must therefore remain explicitly mechanical.

title: Affine Control Interpretation of the Golf Swing: Drift, Input, and Causal Decomposition of Forces - Part I: Theoretical Foundations
section: Force and Torque Taxonomy via the Affine Mapping
text:
Force and Torque Taxonomy via the Affine Mapping
{#sec-taxonomy}
With the drift–input decomposition formalized in Sections~[@sec:ztcf]–[@sec:drift_invariance], we now classify the generalized forces acting within the golfer–club–shaft system. The taxonomy presented here is purely mechanical and applies directly to any control-affine multibody model of the form [ = f(x) + g(x)u. ] It separates forces into distinct causal categories based on their origin in the equations of motion rather than their magnitude or timing.
This taxonomy applies to: - generalized torques at joints,

internal forces transmitted through the kinetic chain,
shaft reaction forces,
hand forces, whether measured or derived. The categories are defined algebraically and can be computed from simulation or from motion-capture data via inverse dynamics.


Total generalized force
At any time (t), inverse dynamics yields the total generalized torque:
\[
  \tau_{\text{total}}(t)
  =
  \text{ID}\big(x(t),\xd(t)\big),
  {#eq-total_tau}
\]
consistent with the equations of motion~\(\eqref{eq:eom_block}\). This total force is the sum of all mechanical contributions and is the unique torque vector that reproduces the observed motion.
We now partition (_{}) into components.


Category 1: Configuration-dependent drift forces
These are forces present due to configuration alone, independent of motion history and independent of torque input. They are obtained from the Zero Velocity Counterfactual (ZVCF) state: [ x^{} = (q,, 0,, ,, 0), ] and are defined as:
\[
  \tau_{\mathrm{ZVCF}}(t)
  =
  \tau_{\text{config}}\big(q(t),\eta(t)\big).
\]
These forces include: - gravitational torques,

elastic shaft forces (restoring stiffness),
geometric coupling forces that depend on configuration,
static interaction forces between rigid and flexible components.

They represent the “static loading” the system experiences if momentarily frozen in place at the same posture.


Category 2: Velocity-dependent drift forces
These are passive forces that depend on velocities but not on applied torques. Subtracting the ZVCF torque from the full drift torque gives:
\[
  \tau_{\mathrm{vel.\,drift}}(t)
  =
  \tau_{\text{drift}}(t) - \tau_{\mathrm{ZVCF}}(t).
  {#eq-veldrift_def}
\]
Velocity-dependent drift forces include: - Coriolis and centrifugal forces,

inertial coupling terms induced by multi-segment motion,
shaft damping forces proportional to (),
any passive joint damping.

These forces can be large—often dominant—in fast regions of the swing (e.g., late downswing).


Category 3: Input (torque-driven) forces
These forces arise solely from the golfer’s active torque input and are defined by:
\[
  \tau_{\mathrm{input}}(t)
  =
  \tau_{\text{total}}(t) - \tau_{\text{drift}}(t).
  {#eq-input_tau_tax}
\]
Here, (_{}) is the passive drift torque evaluated along the actual trajectory, using the same (x(t)) as the total torque:
\[
  \tau_{\text{drift}}(t)
  =
  M_q(q,\eta)\,[a_{\text{drift}}(x(t))]_{1:n}.
\]
By construction, (_{}) contains the mechanical effect of applied torques and nothing else. It is the only category that changes when the golfer changes their motor command.


Category 4: Mixed forces (interaction effects)
Although drift and input contributions add linearly in the equations of motion, [ {} = {} + _{}, ] the external hand forces and internal forces observed along the chain may reflect nonlinear interactions between torque-driven accelerations and drift-induced accelerations. These are best understood by examining: - the ZTCF trajectory (removing input entirely),

the ZVCF state (removing velocity-dependent drift),
the difference between ZTCF and ZVCF forces,
how hand forces change relative to these baselines.

We define:
\[
  \tau_{\mathrm{mixed}}(t)
  =
  \tau_{\text{total}}(t)
  -
  \tau_{\mathrm{ZTCF}}(t)
  -
  \tau_{\mathrm{ZVCF}}(t),
  {#eq-mixed_forces}
\]
understanding that this term does not represent a new physical force, but a nonlinear structural interaction within the model.


Taxonomy summary
Table~[@tab:taxonomy] summarizes the categories.
[Table]


Interpretation and practical use
The taxonomy provides a framework for interpreting joint torques, hand forces, or shaft loads in practice: - Comparing ({}) to ({}) reveals how much of the motion is mechanically self-propelled.

Comparing ({}) to ({}) quantifies inertial loading.
Comparing ({}) to ({}) reveals torque effectiveness.
The interaction term (_{}) helps diagnose when torque amplifies or attenuates passive dynamics.

In simulation (Parts II and III of this project), these categories enable: - decomposition of power flow,

isolation of passive shaft recoil,
identification of torque timing patterns,
mapping of how individual torque bursts shape the club path.

This taxonomy completes the theoretical framework required to interpret forces and torques in the golf swing using control-affine decomposition.

title: Affine Control Interpretation of the Golf Swing: Drift, Input, and Causal Decomposition of Forces - Part I: Theoretical Foundations
text:
Limitations (Theoretical Scope)
{#sec-limitations}
The framework developed in this manuscript provides a mathematically rigorous decomposition of forces in the golf swing within the structure of a nonlinear control-affine mechanical system. It is exact for the chosen model class, but its interpretation is bounded by several theoretical limitations. These limitations do not undermine the decomposition; rather, they define the domain in which its causal statements are valid.

Model-form limitations

Rigid-body anatomical representation.
All anatomical segments of the golfer are modeled as rigid bodies with fixed inertial properties. Compliance in soft tissue, joint capsules, musculotendinous structures, and skin-mounted marker dynamics are excluded. These omissions affect how accurately inverse dynamics relates to true joint torques and internal forces.


Finite-dimensional shaft model.
The shaft is represented using a truncated set of bending modes. Modal truncation introduces approximation error, particularly during high-frequency events (late downswing, impact). Although the affine structure is preserved, the magnitude and timing of drift forces may shift with a more complete flexible-body representation.


No aerodynamic or contact modeling.
Air resistance on the clubhead and shaft, ground–body compliance, and ball–club impact forces are excluded. Since these forces do not enter linearly in torque, adding them would require additional modeling choices and affect the passive drift term.


Holonomic base constraint.
The feet are assumed to be rigidly fixed to the ground. In reality, golfers produce substantial torques through foot pressure modulation, shear forces, and center-of-pressure shifts. These are outside the scope of the current model and will be addressed in subsequent work.



Physiological limitations

Torques as abstract control inputs.
The model uses joint torque inputs (u(t)) as the control channels. This abstracts away: - muscle activation dynamics,

force–velocity and force–length effects,
neural delays,
muscle coordination constraints. Thus, the decomposition is strictly mechanical: it attributes forces to torques, not to muscular effort or neural intent.



State-dependent torque limits.
The feasible set of torques ((x)) may depend on configuration, strength, fatigue, or coordination. These constraints do not break the affine structure but do restrict the set of realizable torque profiles. Interpretations must therefore distinguish between “mechanically possible” and “physiologically plausible.”



Data and parameter limitations

Exact parameter knowledge.
The decomposition assumes perfect knowledge of: - segment masses and inertias,

joint axes and kinematics,
shaft stiffness and damping parameters. Real data introduces parameter uncertainty, which propagates into drift and input estimates. In practice, parameter sensitivity analysis is required for empirical interpretation.



Noise-free kinematics and differentiability.
Inverse dynamics requires accurate positions, velocities, and accelerations. Marker noise, filtering choices, and numerical differentiation introduce error that may distort the partition of drift and input torques.


High-speed phases of motion.
During rapid transitions (late downswing), small errors in acceleration estimation can produce disproportionately large drift torques. These phases require careful filtering and high-frame-rate motion capture.



Conceptual limitations

Interpretation of counterfactuals.
ZTCF and ZVCF are mathematically defined but physically unrealizable states or trajectories. They answer precise mechanical questions but should not be interpreted as physiological or behavioral alternatives available to a real golfer.


No claims about optimality or intent.
The decomposition quantifies how torques shape motion, but it does not imply: - how golfers choose torque policies,

whether they “should” apply different torques,
anything about coaching cues, training goals, or intent. Those require empirical studies (Parts II and III).



Linearity in torque does not imply linearity in outcomes.
Although torque enters linearly in the equations of motion, its effect on the motion is highly nonlinear due to state-dependent inertia and coupling. Therefore, the taxonomy partitions forces cleanly but cannot be interpreted as a “simple additive explanation” of the swing’s motion.



Scope of applicability
Within these assumptions, the decomposition [ {}(t) = {}(x(t)) + _{}(t) ] is exact for the model and provides a well-defined mechanical basis for analyzing forces in the golf swing. Outside this scope, interpretations must be made with explicit reference to model fidelity, parameter uncertainty, and empirical validation.

title: Affine Control Interpretation of the Golf Swing: Drift, Input, and Causal Decomposition of Forces - Part I: Theoretical Foundations
text:
Conclusion and Future Directions
{#sec-conclusion}
This manuscript developed a theoretical framework for decomposing the forces of the golf swing within a nonlinear control-affine mechanical model. By formulating the golfer–club–shaft system as [ = f(x) + g(x)u, ] we derived a clean separation between passive drift forces and torque-driven input forces. The model’s affine structure enabled two mathematically rigorous counterfactual tools—the Zero Torque Counterfactual (ZTCF) and the Zero Velocity Counterfactual (ZVCF)—which isolate the contributions of inertia, configuration, shaft deformation, and applied torques.
The resulting taxonomy (Section~[@sec:taxonomy]) classifies generalized forces into configuration drift, velocity drift, input forces, and nonlinear interaction effects. This provides a principled basis for interpreting torques and hand forces at any instant of the swing. Within the modeling assumptions stated in Section~[@sec:assumptions], the decomposition is analytically exact and reproducible. It offers a mechanical explanation of how the swing evolves over time, distinguishing forces that arise “on their own” from those produced directly by applied torques.
This paper is intentionally limited to theory. No simulation data, parameter estimation, or empirical results have been presented. These will appear in subsequent phases of the project:

Part II: Simulation and Numerical Implementation.
This follow-up manuscript will implement the full drift–input decomposition in a high-fidelity multibody simulation environment, including flexible-shaft modeling, inverse dynamics pipelines, ZTCF trajectory integration, and numerical evaluation of the force taxonomy. It will also study sensitivity to parameter uncertainty and filtering choices for motion derivatives.
Part III: Experimental and Coaching Applications.
The third manuscript will apply the theoretical tools to real motion-capture data. It will quantify drift and input forces in measured swings, examine player-to-player variability, evaluate torque-timing strategies, and identify mechanical signatures associated with clubhead delivery. Practical implications for coaching and equipment design will be evaluated in the context of the “Application of Research” section required by the journal.

Beyond these immediate goals, several broader research directions emerge:

Modeling extensions.
Incorporating foot-ground shear forces, aerodynamic loading, and non-smooth impact dynamics will generalize the framework to capture more phases of the swing.
Physiological modeling.
Embedding simplified muscle activation dynamics or state-dependent torque limits into the control space ((x)) may bridge the gap between mechanical torques and neuromuscular effort.
Optimization and control.
The affine structure lends itself to optimal control formulations aimed at identifying torque policies that reproduce desired trajectories or optimize clubhead delivery metrics.
Data-driven extensions.
The drift–input decomposition may support machine-learning models that predict torque-driven accelerations or infer effort strategies from measured swings. The separation of passive and active forces provides clean targets for such models.
Generalization to other athletic motions.
The same decomposition applies directly to pitching, striking, kicking, and other ballistic sporting movements where passive and torque-driven dynamics interact through coupled multibody systems.

In summary, this manuscript establishes the mathematical foundation for a causal mechanical interpretation of the golf swing. The drift–input decomposition, ZTCF and ZVCF counterfactuals, and the associated force taxonomy provide a rigorous framework for analyzing how torque inputs shape the motion of a compliant multibody system. The subsequent simulation and experimental papers will build on this foundation to connect theory to practice.
The framework developed in this manuscript provides a new mechanical viewpoint for interpreting forces in the golf swing. While the technical details are presented for scientific completeness, the practical impact is straightforward: the approach separates forces that arise naturally from the motion of the body and club (passive drift forces) from forces the golfer must actively create through muscular torque (input forces). This distinction is essential for understanding how players produce clubhead speed, how they sequence their movements, and why some patterns are more efficient than others.
For coaches, the decomposition clarifies several long-standing questions: - When is the club accelerating itself?
Large portions of the downswing may be driven primarily by passive inertia and shaft dynamics rather than muscular effort.

Where is torque actually needed?
By isolating input forces, the model highlights the phases in which golfers must apply torque to shape the club path or manage shaft bending.
Which movement strategies are mechanically efficient?
Comparing a player’s measured forces to the drift-only predictions (ZTCF and ZVCF) reveals whether their torque application amplifies or opposes passive motion.

For equipment professionals, the framework provides a mechanically grounded way to analyze how shaft stiffness, club mass distribution, and player-specific kinematics interact. The drift–input decomposition allows shaft behavior and player torque strategies to be examined independently, improving the matching process between golfers and equipment.
For researchers, the approach offers a reproducible method for quantifying torque effectiveness, evaluating technique variability, and linking high-speed motion capture to causal mechanical explanations of performance.
Overall, the framework enables clearer interpretation of how golfers generate speed, control the club, and use their bodies efficiently—supporting more targeted coaching, equipment fitting, and player development.

title: Affine Control Interpretation of the Golf Swing: Drift, Input, and Causal Decomposition of Forces - Part I: Theoretical Foundations
text:
Mathematical Derivations
{#app:derivations}
This appendix provides detailed derivations supporting the unified control-affine formulation presented in Section~[@sec:affine]. The goal is to show explicitly how the coupled rigid–flexible dynamics produce the affine decomposition [ = f(x) + g(x)u ] and to document all assumptions required for the formulation.

A.1 Coupled rigid–flexible equations of motion
We partition the generalized coordinates into [ q ^{n}, ^{m}, ] where (q) describes the rigid-body degrees of freedom and () contains the modal coordinates of the flexible shaft.
Let
[ v =
\[\begin{bmatrix} \dot{q} \\ \dot{\eta} \end{bmatrix}\]
] denote the generalized velocity.
The equations of motion for the coupled system may be written in compact form:
\[
  M(q,\eta)\,\dot{v}
  +
  C(q,\dot{q},\eta,\dot{\eta})\,v
  +
  G(q)
  +
  F_{s}(\eta,\dot{\eta})
  =
  \begin{bmatrix}
    \tau \\[0.2em]
    0
  \end{bmatrix},
  {#eq-appendix_eom}
\]
where: - (M(q,)) is the full inertia matrix of the rigid–flexible system,

(C(q,,,)) contains Coriolis and centrifugal terms,
(G(q)) contains gravitational torques acting on the rigid-body DOFs,
(F_{s}(,) =
\[\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ K_s \eta + C_s \dot{\eta} \end{bmatrix}\]
) contains shaft restoring and damping forces,
(= B(q),u) is the generalized torque vector induced by the input (u).

The flexible DOFs have no direct torque inputs.


A.2 Block structure of the inertia and Coriolis matrices
The inertia matrix has the block form [ M(q,) =
\[\begin{bmatrix}
    M_{rr}(q,\eta) & M_{rf}(q,\eta) \\
    M_{fr}(q,\eta) & M_{ff}(q,\eta)
  \end{bmatrix}\]
, ] where: - (M_{rr}) is the rigid-body inertia matrix,

(M_{ff}) is the modal inertia matrix for the flexible shaft,
(M_{rf}) and (M_{fr}) represent rigid–flexible coupling.

Similarly, the Coriolis matrix has the block structure: [ C(q,,,) =
\[\begin{bmatrix}
    C_{rr} & C_{rf} \\
    C_{fr} & C_{ff}
  \end{bmatrix}\]
, ] with the usual property that
[ - 2C . ]
These blocks arise from standard manipulator equations extended to include flexible-body contributions.


A.3 Solving for accelerations
Writing ( = [^{T}, ^{T}]^{T}), equation~\(\eqref{eq:appendix_eom}\) becomes:
\[
  M
  \begin{bmatrix}
    \ddot{q} \\ \ddot{\eta}
  \end{bmatrix}
  =
  -
  C
  \begin{bmatrix}
    \dot{q} \\ \dot{\eta}
  \end{bmatrix}
  -
  G(q)
  -
  F_s(\eta,\dot{\eta})
  +
  \begin{bmatrix}
    B(q)\,u \\ 0
  \end{bmatrix}.
  {#eq-appendix_accel_base}
\]
Assuming (M) is invertible (true for all admissible configurations of a well-defined multibody system), we solve for the generalized accelerations:
\[
  \begin{bmatrix}
    \ddot{q} \\ \ddot{\eta}
  \end{bmatrix}
  =
  - M^{-1}
  \left(
    C\,v + G + F_{s}
  \right)
  +
  M^{-1}
  \begin{bmatrix}
    B(q)\,u \\ 0
  \end{bmatrix}.
  {#eq-appendix_accel_split}
\]


A.4 Drift acceleration
We define the drift acceleration as
\[
  a_{\mathrm{drift}}(x)
  =
  -M^{-1}(q,\eta)
  \left(
    C(q,\dot{q},\eta,\dot{\eta})\,v
    + G(q)
    + F_{s}(\eta,\dot{\eta})
  \right).
  {#eq-appendix_drift_def}
\]
All passive mechanical terms are explicitly included: - inertia coupling,

Coriolis and centripetal terms,
gravity,
elastic and damping forces from shaft deformation.

Importantly, [ a_{}(x) u. ]
This constitutes the drift invariance property formalized in Section~[@sec:drift_invariance].


A.5 Input acceleration mapping
The input-driven acceleration is the part proportional to (u):
\[
  a_{\mathrm{input}}(x)\,u
  =
  M^{-1}(q,\eta)
  \begin{bmatrix}
    B(q)\,u \\ 0
  \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Thus the input matrix is:
\[
  A_{\mathrm{input}}(x)
  =
  M^{-1}(q,\eta)
  \begin{bmatrix}
    B(q) \\ 0
  \end{bmatrix}.
  {#eq-appendix_Ainput}
\]
Linearity of the torque input is preserved even in the presence of: - flexible-body modes,

rigid–flexible coupling,
configuration-dependent (B(q)),
velocity-dependent (C) terms.



A.6 First-order state-space (affine) form
Define the full state [ x =
\[\begin{bmatrix}
    q \\ \dot{q} \\ \eta \\ \dot{\eta}
  \end{bmatrix}\]
. ]
The first-order dynamics follow directly from the definitions: [ =
\[\begin{bmatrix}
    \dot{q} \\ \ddot{q} \\ \dot{\eta} \\ \ddot{\eta}
  \end{bmatrix}\]
= f(x) + g(x)u, ] with
\[
  f(x)
  =
  \begin{bmatrix}
    \dot{q} \\[0.2em]
    \left[a_{\mathrm{drift}}(x)\right]_{1:n} \\[0.2em]
    \dot{\eta} \\[0.2em]
    \left[a_{\mathrm{drift}}(x)\right]_{n+1:n+m}
  \end{bmatrix},
\]
\[
  g(x)
  =
  \begin{bmatrix}
    0 \\[0.2em]
    \left[A_{\mathrm{input}}(x)\right]_{1:n,:} \\[0.2em]
    0 \\[0.2em]
    \left[A_{\mathrm{input}}(x)\right]_{n+1:n+m,:}
  \end{bmatrix}.
\]
This establishes the nonlinear control-affine structure used throughout the manuscript.


A.7 Notes on coordinate choices
The derivations above are independent of the coordinate representation used for the rigid-body DOFs, provided: - the coordinates are minimal and smooth, or

redundant coordinates are supplemented with constraint forces.

The formulation is consistent with: - Denavit–Hartenberg (DH) joint coordinates,

spatial vector formulations,
exponential coordinates for rigid-body motion,
Euler angles (with appropriate domain restrictions),
quaternion-based internal representations (converted to minimal coordinates for dynamics).

The drift and input mappings depend only on the mechanical structure and remain unchanged by a different choice of coordinates or frames.


A.8 Summary
The derivations in this appendix demonstrate explicitly that: - the golfer–club–shaft system admits a nonlinear control-affine representation,

drift forces arise solely from passive dynamics,
input forces arise solely from the torque inputs,
all rigid–flexible coupling remains in the drift term,
counterfactual constructions (ZTCF and ZVCF) follow naturally from the structure.

This provides the mathematical backbone for the force decomposition and torque taxonomy developed in the main text.

section: Modal Approximation for the Flexible Shaft
text:
Modal Approximation for the Flexible Shaft
{#app:modal}
This appendix details the finite-dimensional modal approximation used to model shaft deformation in the unified rigid–flexible dynamics of the golfer–club system. The goal is to show how a continuous beam model reduces to the generalized modal coordinates (^{m}) used in Section~[@sec:affine], and why this representation preserves the linearity of the torque input in the final control-affine form.

B.1 Continuous beam model
The golf shaft is modeled as a uniform Euler–Bernoulli beam of length (L), with transverse displacement field [ w(s,t), s , ] where (s) is the arc-length coordinate from the butt (grip) end. For small deflections, the beam equation is
\[
  \rho A \,\frac{\partial^2 w}{\partial t^2}
  + c_b \frac{\partial w}{\partial t}
  + EI \,\frac{\partial^4 w}{\partial s^4}
  = f_{\mathrm{base}}(s,t),
  {#eq-beam_equation}
\]
where: - (A) is the linear mass density,

(c_b) is distributed damping,
(E I) is the bending rigidity,
(f_{}(s,t)) contains forces transmitted from the handle motion.

Boundary conditions depend on grip modeling. We assume: [ w(0,t) = 0, w_s(0,t) = 0, ] for a clamped handle, and free-tip conditions at (s=L): [ EI,w_{ss}(L,t) = 0, EI,w_{sss}(L,t) = 0. ]
These constraints define the mode shapes used in the modal expansion.


B.2 Modal expansion
The transverse displacement is approximated using a finite set of vibration modes:
\[
  w(s,t)
  \approx
  \sum_{i=1}^{m} \phi_i(s)\,\eta_i(t),
  {#eq-modal_expansion}
\]
where: - (_i(s)) are the eigenfunctions of the beam operator with the boundary conditions above,

(_i(t)) are the modal amplitudes,
(m) is the number of modes retained.

The mode shapes satisfy the eigenvalue problem: [ EI ,_i”” = _i^2 A ,_i, ] with orthogonality relations [ _0^L A ,_i(s),j(s),ds = {ij}. ]
Substituting~\(\eqref{eq:modal_expansion}\) into the beam equation and projecting onto each (_i) yields the modal equations of motion.


B.3 Modal equations of motion
The projected dynamics have the form:
\[
  \ddot{\eta}_i
  + 2\,\zeta_i \omega_i\,\dot{\eta}_i
  + \omega_i^2 \eta_i
  =
  Q_i(q,\dot{q}),
  {#eq-modal_eom_single}
\]
for (i = 1,,m), where: - (_i) is the natural frequency of mode (i),

(_i) is the modal damping ratio (derived from (c_b)),
(Q_i(q,)) are generalized modal forces induced by handle motion.

Collecting terms, [ + C_s + K_s = Q(q,), ] where: [ K_s = (_1^2,,_m^2), C_s = (2_1_1,,2_m_m). ]
These matrices match those used in Section~[@sec:affine], where the shaft forces enter the drift term.


B.4 Rigid–flexible coupling
Motion of the hands introduces base excitation into the beam. If (r_h(q)) denotes the handle position, the kinematic constraint yields: [ w(0,t) = r_h(q(t)) f_{}(s,t) _h(q,,). ]
Projected modal forcings then take the form: [ Q(q,) = - M_{fr}(q,), - C_{fr}(q,,,), - , ] matching the coupling seen in the full equations of motion.
Critically: [ Q(q,) u. ]
All torque influence on the shaft is mediated through rigid-body acceleration.


B.5 Preservation of linear torque input
From the full equations of motion: [ M(q,), + C(q,,,),v + G(q) + F_s(,) =
\[\begin{bmatrix}
    B(q)u \\ 0
  \end{bmatrix}\]
, ] the modal forces enter entirely through the drift term: [ F_s(,) =
\[\begin{bmatrix}
    0 \\
    K_s \eta + C_s \dot{\eta}
  \end{bmatrix}\]
. ]
Because (u) appears only in the block (B(q)u) associated with rigid-body torques: [ u . ]
Hence: [ The modal representation does not create any nonlinear torque dependence. ]
All flexible-body dynamics remain embedded in the drift vector field (f(x)).


B.6 Influence of mode truncation
Using (m < ) modes introduces model reduction error: - High-frequency shaft vibration is omitted.

Tip deflection accuracy depends on (m).
Stiffness estimates become approximate near impact.

However, the structure of the drift–input decomposition is preserved for any (m).
Increasing (m) simply increases the dimension of the drift term, never the form of the input term.


B.7 Summary
The modal shaft model presented here: - originates from a continuous beam,

reduces to a finite-dimensional ODE system via orthogonal mode projection,
produces stiffness and damping forces that appear only in the drift,
preserves the linearity of torque input,
maintains the control-affine structure central to the force and torque taxonomy.

This makes the modal approximation both computationally efficient and theoretically compatible with the full decomposition presented in the main text.
